answer: Node2vec is a static, batch method. It learns embeddings for a fixed graph by running biased random walks (controlled by the return parameter p and in-out parameter q) and then training a skip-gram model with negative sampling. It does not describe how to handle a network that changes over time. Incorporating new nodes or edges means rerunning the walks and retraining on the whole graph. The streaming variant treats the network as a sequence of arriving edges or nodes and updates the existing embeddings incrementally, without full retraining, so new nodes can be embedded and the embeddings kept current as the graph grows. The capability it adds that node2vec does not explicitly mention is this online or incremental updating of embeddings for a growing (streaming) graph, which allows new nodes and edges to be embedded on arrival at much lower cost. I am not certain which specific streaming node2vec paper is meant, so these details are general to that class of method.
